1:
Gill hears in the opening formula either a continuation or a fresh start after some pause, and adds that the law, like the rest, bound Israel and such as were proselyted to them. Henry treats the same words as a seam. The laws of the first three chapters seem delivered at one time; here begin the statutes of another day, spoken from the throne of glory between the cherubim, and Wesley keeps just that much. What follows, Henry says, is more strictly new than anything before it. Burnt offerings, meat offerings and peace offerings had been made before the law was given at Sinai, the patriarchs having respect in them to sin; but the law being added because of transgressions, men were put into a way of atoning more particularly by sacrifice, which more than any other ceremonial institution was a shadow of good things to come, the substance being Christ and that one offering by which he put away sin. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the grammar. The earlier offerings are spoken of as familiar, in the voluntary formula if any man of you bring; here the words are if a soul shall sin, let him bring, and the sin offering enters as a new injunction. Calvin explains why it comes first in importance: without reconciliation there is no intercourse between men and God, who deservedly abominates the race for the corruption of our nature, so the whole hope of salvation rests on the remedies provided for propitiating him.

That the ritual is graded by rank is stated at the outset. Calvin notes that one kind of victim is required of a king, another of the priests, another of ordinary persons, with regard had to the poor, that they may not be burdened by so great an expense as the rich. Keil and Delitzsch set out the same four classes, the anointed priest, the congregation, the prince and the common people, and observe that the ritual differed for each in the animal, the sprinkling of the blood and the treatment of the flesh, according to the offerer's position in the kingdom of God; for the last class regard was paid to circumstances too, so the offering could be scaled to his ability. Clarke lists the chapter's divisions in the same order.

What ignorance covers here is the question the writers spend most on. Ellicott gives the plain sense first, that the man acted inadvertently and did not know at the time he was transgressing but recognised it afterwards, and adds the four conditions the second Temple attached: the sin must be involuntary rather than of set purpose, against a negative command, consisting in acts and not in words, and of a kind that if done intentionally would have brought excision. Calvin narrows it likewise, denying that all kinds of ignorance are included and taking the Hebrew for a sin into which a perplexed mind has been driven by some passion, through thoughtlessness or imprudence. Wesley argues the limit from practicality: if every daily infirmity had required an offering, most sinners could not have borne the charge, nor the altar received so many, nor the priests managed so infinite a work. He asks too why negative commands are singled out, and answers that affirmative precepts do not bind men so strictly and constantly. Clarke draws the sharpest consequence. A man's ignorance is no excuse; as soon as the transgression comes to his knowledge he must bring the sacrifice, and if he refuses he sins obstinately and wilfully, so that nothing remains for him but a fearful looking for of judgment, which Clarke takes to be the case the apostle has in view. Henry adds the boundary on the other side: sin is the transgression of the divine law, and the wits or wills of men cannot make that a sin which God's law has not made one.
3:
That the law begins at the top is taken as deliberate. Gill notes that the Targums and the Greek both read the anointed priest for the high priest, and draws the apostle's inference: the law made men high priests who had infirmity, even sinful infirmities, needing to offer for themselves as well as for others, by which it appeared perfection could not be had under that priesthood and it was proper it should cease. Ellicott puts it positively: by adducing the chief of the order as its first instance, the law shows him a frail being exposed to the same infirmities as the laity, and so forestalls any claim of spiritual superiority. He adds that the title belongs to this book alone, where it occurs four times, the rest of the Pentateuch and Joshua saying the great priest. Keil and Delitzsch explain the title from the completeness of the unction consecrating him to office, and Wesley notes he was not complete in the dignity until anointed. Calvin turns rank into obligation: the more illustrious the dignity, the more closely should the life be conformed to holiness, so a failing tolerable in others grew reprehensible in him, which is why a costlier victim was demanded. That obligation, he says, now reaches every minister and pastor, not to ransom themselves with a calf but to shun every fault and press harder after holiness.

The clause according to the sin of the people is read two ways. Taken as comparison, it means he erred as any layman might, which Wesley says implies God expected more circumspection from him. Taken as consequence, the Hebrew runs to the guilt of the people. Clarke reports critics who render it if the anointed priest shall lead the people to sin, glossing it as the shepherd straying and the flock following. Keil and Delitzsch refer it to his official standing as the nation's representative before God, not merely to his private relation to him. Calvin allows the same, that he corrupted the nation by his example, and Wesley gives both, treating the second as an aggravation, since such a fall commonly brings guilt and punishment on men infected or scandalised by it. On the victim all agree the size answers to the office: Wesley notes it equals what is brought for the whole nation, and Keil that the ox is the largest beast on the list, the offerer filling the highest post in Israel.

Of the ceremony Calvin says frankly that the sprinkling, the pouring and the burning of the fat run as elsewhere, the tenth verse proving the usual forms were kept. What needed exact prescribing was the awkwardness of the case, since it might seem absurd that a guilty man should come before God to work reconciliation. His answer is that the law of the priesthood was inviolable and no further mediators could lawfully be appointed, so God stretched his grace over the fault rather than let men look elsewhere for pardon; the sprinkling before the Lord taught onlookers that at the sight of the victim their transgressions were hidden and buried, to come no more into remembrance. Gill observes that he took the blood himself and not by deputy, being his own suppliant, and that the sprinkling went by the right hand, the rabbinic canons counting the left invalid. Clarke sets out its three applications: sprinkled seven times before the veil, smeared on the horns of the incense altar, and the residue poured at the foot of the brazen one. Ellicott marks the movement indoors, from the court where the beast was killed into the tent of meeting, and Wesley observes that such entry was neither required nor allowed on any other occasion, possibly to mark how grave the offence was. Keil notes the fat portions lifted off match those of the peace offering.
13:
Who is meant by the whole congregation is disputed. Wesley takes it for the body of the people, or the greater part, their rulers concurring, and Gill begins the same way, all Israel or the bulk of them, misled by the ignorant teaching of judges whose instruction makes the nation err; but he reports that Jarchi and others understand the sanhedrim, the bench of seventy-one. Ellicott sets both readings side by side. On the plain construction the two words rendered congregation and assembly denote one body used interchangeably, so that those who inadvertently offended are those who afterwards recognised the fault; but the interpretation current in the time of Christ made them the great Sanhedrin, representatives who might through error proclaim a mistaken decree. Gill quotes Ainsworth's terse comment on the verse, that the church may err.

Henry builds his exposition on that comment. This is the law for expiating a national guilt, and it supposes that leaders may mistake the law and lead their people astray, the offering being brought once the error is found, that wrath may not fall on all. God will always have a church on earth, Henry says, but he never promised it should be infallible or perfectly pure from corruption this side of heaven. The offence he imagines is a common usage taken up on the presumption that it was lawful, which upon later search proved otherwise; and neither the commonness of the practice, received perhaps by tradition, nor the general opinion of its lawfulness excuses them from bringing an atonement. Ellicott describes the case identically, and both he and Clarke reach for the same instance, the men who after the long fight with the Philistines flew on the spoil and ate with the blood, which Clarke connects with Saul's rash adjuration cursing any man who ate before evening. Calvin approaches it through the phrase if the thing be hid, which seems to mark a different sort of ignorance from the earlier. He allows that it covers the infirmity of men blinded for a season, who do not search themselves and so slumber, whereas an honest examination would make conscience smite them at once. A whole people, he says, may miss its own sin while dealing with itself too gently; and the point of the law is that though nothing at first rouses them, once awakened to acknowledge the fault they must still propitiate God, or they would make their error a cloak.

The ritual repeats the earlier case, and Calvin explains why: the same victim serves, because the man who entered the sanctuary in the name of all and presented the tribes before God stood for the whole body. Ellicott notes the animal is the same as for the anointed priest, and though the text does not repeat it the beast must be without blemish; Wesley adds from Numbers that where the fault was merely the omission of a ceremonial duty a kid of the goats sufficed. Ellicott also disposes of a misreading of the phrase about bringing the bullock before the tent of meeting. It no more means that the thousands of Israel each lay hold of the victim and carry it than the earlier wording means the high priest carried his own; it is the ordinary Hebrew idiom for causing a thing to be brought, and Ellicott would have thought the explanation superfluous had mistaken arguments not been drawn from it. On the laying on of hands the reports differ in number. Henry has the elders act as representatives and agents of the people, three at the least; Clarke follows Maimonides for three of the Sanhedrin, acting in the name of all; Gill collects the range of opinion, two at least, some saying three and some five, with three of the sanhedrim the more generally received view, though the Targum of Jonathan makes them the twelve rulers of the twelve tribes.
20:
Who the ruler is nobody settles. Gill derives the Hebrew from a root meaning to lift up or bear, so the man is one raised above others, or one carrying the weight of government; he reports Aben Ezra allowing the head of a household or tribe, the Talmud making it a tribal prince such as Nachson the son of Amminadab, and Maimonides and Gersom holding a king is meant, David being called a prince. Clarke thinks any political dignity may be covered, granting that the rabbins read it of the king; Keil and Delitzsch take it for the head of a tribe or tribal division. Ellicott admits the word carries all three senses, then argues from a detail nobody else notices. In the other cases the fault is simply against any commandment of the Lord, whereas here alone the text says of the Lord his God; from that addition the second Temple drew its reading, that the man is one over whom God alone is exalted, answerable to no one else. Calvin cuts the knot differently. The singular is used, but no law had yet made one man ruler, so Moses must mean heads and governors generally, named because men in authority do more harm by a bad example than private persons can.

Henry seizes the same possessive and makes it the lesson. God takes notice of the sins of rulers; those who have power to call others to account are themselves accountable to the ruler of rulers, for high as they are, there is a higher than they. The commandment broken is called the commandment of the Lord his God: he is a prince to other men, Henry says, but let him know that the Lord is a God to him. Calvin draws the same conclusion from the scale of the offerings. A governor was discharged by a smaller victim than the anointed priest or the nation required, yet a costlier one than a private man brought, the object being that men in office should keep the more carefully from every transgression, whereas they are otherwise apt to indulge themselves, as though rank allowed a wider licence.

Wesley notes only that the bullock called the first here is the one brought for the priest's own sin. How the fault comes to light is treated as the turning point. Gill allows either that others informed him or that he called his own act to mind and weighed it against the law; Keil supposes someone drew his attention to it; Ellicott corrects the last clause, which is not and is guilty but and acknowledges his guilt, as the same version rightly renders the verb in Hosea. Henry makes the moment a duty. The discovery comes by the check of conscience or the reproof of friends, and both, he says, even the best of us should not merely submit to but be thankful for; what we have done amiss we ought to be desirous to find out. He turns it into a daily petition, that God would teach what we do not see and show wherein we have erred, so that having fallen into sin through ignorance we may not through ignorance lie still in it. On the offering the accounts agree. Henry marks three ways it falls short of the earlier ritual: a kid of the goats rather than a bullock, no blood carried into the tabernacle, and the whole of it bestowed on the brazen altar. Clarke notes the rites are nearly as before except that the fat was burnt as in the peace offering, and Keil gives the sequence, the hand laid on the beast, the killing at the place of burnt offering, the blood on the horns and the rest poured at the foot, adding that the buck-goat is named again and again for a sin offering, for the tribe-princes and for the nation at its feasts.
27:
The fourth case is the ordinary Israelite, and the writers begin by fixing who that is. Gill renders the Hebrew as one soul of the people of the earth, a single man distinguished from the congregation, neither high priest nor prince nor king, but a common priest or Levite or lay Israelite; from which he takes occasion to say that no man is free from sin, all ranks and degrees, high and low, rich and poor, in office civil or ecclesiastical, sinning continually either ignorantly or willingly, and that Christ is a sacrifice for all sins and for every sort of sinner. Clarke translates the phrase people of the land and thinks it may reach the very lowest, the labouring or agricultural classes. Ellicott defines it by exclusion, any member of the congregation who is neither the anointed priest nor the ruler already named, and repeats his correction of the closing clause, that the words mean not and is guilty but and acknowledges his guilt.

Henry lays the two laws side by side and finds only two differences. A private man might bring either a kid or a lamb where the ruler was confined to a kid, and the ruler's beast had to be male where the commoner's was female; in every other circumstance of the offering the two agree. Wesley gives the reason for the lesser victim, that the sin of such a person was less than the sin of a ruler; Ellicott adds that the Hebrew word is feminine and that a she-goat, being of smaller value, suited the means of ordinary people. What Henry draws from the case is that the meanest are as much within the law as the greatest. Jeremiah supposes the poor not so likely as the great men to know the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God, and yet if they sin through ignorance they must bring an offering; even sins of ignorance need atoning for by sacrifice. To plead, when we are charged with sin, that we did it ignorantly and under the surprise of temptation will not bring us off, Henry says, unless we have an interest in that greater plea, that Christ has died. He turns it into the prayer of David, who was himself a ruler, to be cleansed from secret faults, the errors a man does not understand or is not aware of in himself; and he observes that as the greatest are not above the censure of this law, the meanest are not beneath its notice.

Clarke takes the close of the chapter as the place to recapitulate, and states the whole procedure in one sequence. For every transgression of this kind, whether by the people, the prince or the priest, an expiatory offering had to be made; the man who had sinned brought his victim to the door of the tabernacle and laid his hands on its head, acknowledging the sacrifice to be his and that he needed it for his offence. By that act he was reckoned to confess the sin, the sin was reckoned as transferred to the animal, and its blood was then spilt to make the atonement. Clarke will not let the institution rest there. Such ordinances, he says, could not be considered as terminating in themselves, and necessarily had reference to something beyond. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the mechanics, tracing the same order for this offerer as for the ruler: the hand laid on the head, the killing at the place of the burnt offering, the blood taken with the finger and put upon the horns of the altar, the remainder poured out at its foot, and all the fat taken away as it is taken from the sacrifice of peace offerings and burnt for a sweet savour, whereupon the priest makes atonement and it is forgiven him.
32:
The sheep is offered as an alternative to the goat, and the two commentators who notice it disagree about what the alternative means. Ellicott renders the word sheep rather than lamb and takes the provision as a concession to means: those unable to bring a goat might offer a female sheep, the less valuable animal, provided it was without blemish. Gill reports the opposite reckoning from the Jewish writers, who observe that a lamb is elsewhere always named before a goat as the more excellent of the two in its kind, and who infer from its standing after the goat here that the two are held equally alike. Ellicott explains why the sheep should be given a paragraph of its own when the ritual is identical: the fat tail had to be burned with the rest, and that required separate mention. Gill notes only that the hand is laid on the head of the lamb as on the head of the goat, and, following the Targum, that it is the right hand.

Two small points close the chapter. Wesley observes that the command to burn them uses a plural because the fat was of several kinds, and that the Hebrew reads upon the offerings made by fire, meaning together with them or after them, since the burnt offerings were to have the first place. Ellicott makes the same correction and explains the practice behind it. The daily morning sacrifice was offered first and lay burning on the altar all the forenoon, so no fresh or special fire was kindled for what followed; the later offering was laid upon the fire sacrifices already there. He ends on a distinction that runs back through the whole chapter. The flesh of the sin offering for a ruler and for a private Israelite was not carried out and burnt beyond the camp, as the flesh was in the two earlier cases, but fell to the priests as their perquisite and was eaten by them. That is consistent, Ellicott says, with the rule that the sinner who brought the offering could not partake of it: the priest was accordingly forbidden to eat of what he offered for his own sin, and forbidden also to eat of the congregation's sin offering, because he was himself a member of the congregation.
